questions.q: Which inequality defines a convex function f on a convex domain?
options: f(θx + (1−θ)y) ≥ θf(x) + (1−θ)f(y) for all θ∈[0,1]
f(θx + (1−θ)y) ≤ θf(x) + (1−θ)f(y) for all θ∈[0,1]
f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y)
f(x) ≤ 0 for all x in the domain
questions.explain: Convexity means the function's value on the segment between two points never exceeds the straight-line interpolation between the function's values at those points.

questions.q: What is the standard second-order test for convexity of a twice-differentiable function?
options: The gradient is zero everywhere
The Hessian is positive semi-definite everywhere on the domain
The function is bounded above
The Hessian has a negative determinant
questions.explain: A twice-differentiable function is convex on a convex domain if and only if its Hessian matrix is positive semi-definite at every point in that domain.

questions.q: Why is portfolio variance f(w) = wᵀΣw always a convex function of w?
options: Because expected returns are always positive
Because its Hessian is 2Σ, and a covariance matrix Σ is always positive semi-definite
Because portfolio weights must sum to one
Because variance is always less than one
questions.explain: The Hessian of wᵀΣw is the constant matrix 2Σ. Since Σ is a covariance matrix, it is positive semi-definite by construction (no variance can be negative), so the quadratic form is convex everywhere.

questions.q: What key guarantee does convexity provide for an optimization problem?
options: The optimal value is always zero
Gradient descent will never need more than one step
Any local minimum over a convex feasible set is also the global minimum
The problem has no stationary points
questions.explain: For a convex function minimized over a convex set, every local minimum is guaranteed to be a global minimum, eliminating the risk of getting trapped in a worse local optimum.

questions.q: Why does maximizing the Sharpe ratio (μᵀw − r_f) / sqrt(wᵀΣw) require extra care compared to minimizing variance directly?
options: Because expected returns μ are always convex
Because the Sharpe ratio, a ratio involving a square-root term, is not naturally concave in w and generally needs a convex reformulation
Because the Sharpe ratio has no mathematical definition
Because risk-free rates are never known
questions.explain: Unlike plain variance minimization, the Sharpe ratio is a ratio of a linear term and the square root of a convex term, which is not automatically concave; practitioners typically reformulate it into a convex program before solving.
